full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** The first pass guessed the right general area but put the behaviour in the wrong class, so I'm overturning it.

**Closest match.** There is a matching paper: arXiv 2609.16821, "Odd diffusion and power-law correlations in chiral mass-transport processes" (submitted 15 September 2026). I only read it through a third-party summary page (Pith), not the arXiv text itself. That page says the authors introduce a class of exactly solvable chiral mass-transport models (generalized KMP) on a square lattice and show that odd diffusion alone, without anisotropy, produces algebraic density correlations decaying as ~ |r|^{-4}. Your rule matches it closely: the model relies on coordinated three-site L-shaped moves to generate odd diffusion. Keeping a fixed fraction plus a random share of the rest is the generalized KMP (Kipnis–Marchioro–Presutti) update.

**How each observed feature lines up:**
- **Decay exponent of 4:** reported. The summary says the power law comes from the interplay between the off-diagonal components of the diffusion tensor (the odd-diffusion coefficient $D^{(\text{odd}$) and the off-diagonal components of the mobility tensor.
- **One turning strength that minimises fluctuations, and the square-root cusp:** reported. The zero-wavenumber structure factor (compressibility) decreases with increasing chirality at small odd diffusion, then increases and develops a square-root cusp singularity at a maximal admissible odd-diffusion strength, revealing a dual role of chirality in regulating density fluctuations.
- **x/y ratio of 1.0:** the correlations have an angular dependence, but I couldn't see its exact form in the summary. A four-fold pattern would give equal values along x and y, so the ratio is consistent with the paper but doesn't by itself show the pattern is isotropic. Worth checking directly.

**Why the first pass was wrong.** It called this Class-I hyperuniformity driven by centre-of-mass conservation. Your rule doesn't conserve centre of mass: the L-shaped moves carry mass a net distance. It also isn't hyperuniform. The quantity being minimised is a finite compressibility at zero wavenumber, and it rises again towards the cusp, so it never goes to zero. The r⁻⁴ decay is the generic power-law correlation of driven systems, produced here by odd diffusion. The centre-of-mass mechanism belongs to the related Hazra–Chakraborty–Mukherjee–Pradhan paper, which shows that for d>1, the steady-state static density-density and "activity"-density correlation functions in the thermodynamic limit typically decay as ∼1/r(d+2). A talk by Pradhan presents centre-of-mass-conserving and chiral dynamics as two important classes of dynamics. Your system belongs to the chiral one.

**Is it a real effect or an artifact?** Real. All four features are predicted analytically by an exactly solvable theory, and nothing points to a frozen state, numerical blow-up or random colouring. I can't tell from the summary whether the paper used exactly 40% and 60% retention, but the behaviour doesn't depend on that.
